sources.title: Human History Map, historical-basemap civilization index
sources.note: Exact repository record for timurid-emirates: Timurid Emirates, circa 1492 to 1530; the separately carded predecessor timurid-empire ends at the atlas boundary in 1492.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1400 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded predecessor timurid-empire feature: one polygon, one ring and 362 positions, with a much larger extent than the later Timurid Emirates locator.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1492 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one polygon, one ring and 53 positions; Herat, Mashhad, Balkh, Kabul and Bukhara test inside its coarse outline.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1500 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded exact target feature: one polygon, one ring and 53 positions; topology scaling causes only tiny coordinate differences from the 1492 outline.

sources.title: Human History Map, world-1530 historical basemap topology
sources.note: Decoded handoff snapshot contains Safavid, Mughal, Khiva and Bukara Khanate features over different portions of the former locator, rather than one exact successor.

sources.title: The Timurids in Transition: Turko-Persian Politics and Acculturation in Medieval Iran
sources.note: University of Toronto scholarly book description situates late Timurid politics, Persian administration, agrarian revenues and endowed institutions, especially under Sultan Husayn Bayqara from 1469 to 1506.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Babor, Zahir-al-Din Mohammad
sources.note: Scholarly biography follows Babur from Fergana and repeated Samarkand struggles through Kabul in 1504, Panipat in 1526 and his death in 1530.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Hosayn Bayqara
sources.note: Scholarly biography covers the last important Timurid ruler in Khorasan, his sons, rebellions, cultural patronage, Chaghatay writing and the 1506 succession crisis.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat III: History, Medieval Period
sources.note: Scholarly city history describes fragmented Timurid rule, Husayn Bayqara’s flourishing court, family conflict, Herat’s 1507 surrender and later Safavid occupation.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Abu’l-Khayrids
sources.note: Scholarly dynastic study explains Muhammad Shaybani’s Uzbek coalition, Central Asian conquests, political traditions and the displacement of Timurid princes in Transoxiana.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Safavids
sources.note: Scholarly overview records the Shaybanid capture of Khorasan, Shah Ismail’s defeat of Muhammad Shaybani in 1510 and Safavid occupation of Herat.

sources.title: Babur, chapter 7: Padshahliq, Governance in Hindustan
sources.note: Cambridge scholarly chapter examines Babur’s 1526 conquest, the challenge of governing Hindustan and the foreignness of his Central Asian entourage in its new setting.

sources.title: Princes of the Mughal Empire, prologue
sources.note: Cambridge scholarly prologue treats Babur’s death and Humayun’s succession within the continuing Timurid-Mughal problem of princes, inheritance and imperial sovereignty.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, Intimate Landscapes in Uzbekistan
sources.note: Museum research essay traces young Babur’s early seizure and loss of Samarkand and relates his ambitions to family competition and remembered Timurid landscapes.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, From Peshawar to Panipat
sources.note: Museum research essay explains Kabul’s limited revenues, Babur’s campaigns and alliances, the violence at Bajaur, garden building and the advance toward Panipat.

sources.title: University of Washington Silk Road Seattle, Memoirs of Zehir-Ed-Din Muhammed Babur
sources.note: University primary-source selections from the Baburnama preserve Babur’s observations about fruits, grain, water, hunting, meals, hunger, illness, sport, poetry and music.

sources.title: Project Gutenberg, The Bābur-nāma in English, translated by Annette Beveridge
sources.note: Searchable public-domain translation of Babur’s memoir provides primary accounts of travel, hunts, horse races, family events, gardens, food, poetry and political life.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, Friends and Enemies
sources.note: Museum interpretation uses Babur’s memoir to discuss women relatives’ advice, his mother’s authority, his first marriage and unusually candid accounts of adolescent feeling.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, Istalif: Babur’s Favorite Garden
sources.note: Museum research essay uses the memoir to reconstruct garden outings with companions, poetry, music and wine, while also discussing family influence and succession.

sources.title: Timurid Women: Agency and Power in the Palatial Space
sources.note: Scholarly article surveys Timurid women’s architectural patronage and public visibility, including Gawhar Shad’s madrasa and a 1506 women’s gathering at Husayn Bayqara’s madrasa.

sources.title: Invisible East, Document of the Month 6.2: Timurid Epistolary Collections
sources.note: Oxford project essay translates and transcribes late Timurid Persian model letters about marriage coercion, bathhouse rent, sewage flooding, irrigation, grain, petitions and postal relays.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Clothing IX: In the Mongol and Timurid Periods
sources.note: Scholarly material-culture survey describes textiles, shirts, trousers, robes, belts, boots and turbans while warning that paintings and sparse surviving garments require careful interpretation.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Economy VI: In the Timurid Period
sources.note: Scholarly survey covers irrigation, farming, fruit, grain, pastoral exchange, urban craft production, caravan trade, endowed property and late Timurid monetary strain.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Herat IV: Topography and Urban Development
sources.note: Scholarly urban study describes Herat’s Timurid expansion, bazaars, suburbs, canals, cultivated land, gardens and the Juy-e Soltani irrigation project.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Bagh IV: In Afghanistan
sources.note: Scholarly garden history identifies Babur’s Kabul gardens, altered watercourses, springs, terraces and their uses for receptions, celebrations, gifts and convalescence.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Garden III: Mughal Gardens
sources.note: Scholarly garden history explains how Babur carried Timurid garden practices into South Asia and records reservoirs, channels, plantings and fruit at early Mughal gardens.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, Babur and His World: A Culture of Books
sources.note: Museum interpretation explains elite expectations in poetry, calligraphy and painting, the status of Bihzad and Sultan Ali Mashhadi, and intricate cut-paper book arts.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, Nasta‘liq: The Genius of Persian Calligraphy
sources.note: Museum exhibition research describes nasta‘liq calligraphy, Sultan Ali Mashhadi, large jali writing and qita‘i cut-paper compositions around 1500.

sources.title: Metropolitan Museum of Art, Divan of Sultan Husain Mirza, 1500
sources.note: Museum catalogue identifies a Chaghatay Turkish poetry manuscript made at Herat in 1500 with colored papers, gold decoration and calligraphy by Sultan Ali Mashhadi.

sources.title: Aga Khan Museum, Manuscript of the Lights of Canopus
sources.note: Museum catalogue describes Husayn Vaiz Kashifi’s Persian animal-fable collection, composed at Herat in 1499 to 1500 and dedicated to a Timurid amir.

sources.title: British Museum, brass ewer made in Herat in 1498
sources.note: Museum object record dates an inlaid brass jug to 11 April 1498 at Herat and records its Persian inscriptions, maker and silver-and-gold decoration.

sources.title: Library of Congress, Baburnama digital collection record
sources.note: Library catalogue explains that Babur composed his memoir in Chaghatay Turkish and that it later circulated through Persian translation and illustrated Mughal manuscripts.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kanaqah
sources.note: Scholarly institutional history describes Ali Shir Navai’s Ikhlasiyya complex at Herat with mosque, school, Sufi lodge, hospital, bath, residence, garden and large soup kitchen.

sources.title: Wellcome Collection, two medical works copied at Herat in 1491
sources.note: Public museum catalogue identifies an illustrated Arabic medical manuscript copied in Herat in 1491, written in nasta‘liq with black and red ink and about 200 images.

sources.title: Medical Practice in Medieval Persia, University of Edinburgh doctoral thesis
sources.note: Academic thesis synthesizes chronicles and manuscripts, noting five reported Herat hospitals and student attendance at Ali Shir Navai’s hospital under practicing physicians.

sources.title: The Iranian Hammams in the Ilkhanid and Timurid Periods
sources.note: Academic architectural study reconstructs Timurid bathhouse spaces, heating, hot and cold water, changing rooms, massage areas, foot washing and small toilets, with survival limits.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Iranica, India XVI: Indo-Persian Historiography
sources.note: Scholarly historiographic overview identifies Babur’s 1530 death, Humayun’s succession and a Herati physician’s 1530 Persian hygiene poem dedicated to Babur.

Imported border coordinates remain unchanged. Historical events and map coverage are distinguished in prose; see batchIdentityNotes for conflicts.

proposedOverrides.summary: Rival Timurid courts, Herat’s fall, Babur’s Kabul survival and the Mughal transformation, with family, food, learning, medicine, sanitation and authentic Persian.

batchIdentityNotes: Exact atlas id audited: timurid-emirates, circa 1492 to 1530.
The 1492 and 1500 exact target geometries are near-identical coarse locators, not claims of stable borders.
The existing timurid-empire card is a distinct predecessor ending at the atlas 1492 boundary.
Herat’s court ended in 1507, while Babur’s branch continued through Kabul into Mughal India; 1530 is a map handoff, not simultaneous extinction.
